claim: ABORT DISK puts a disk into the STOPPED state, substate HARDDOWN, but leaves the disk process running.
With the FORCED attribute the command executes without any interaction with the user, even if files are open on the device.
Using FORCED on a physical disk requires first stopping all processes that use the disk for object code or swap files, otherwise a %5113 halt could occur.
STOP TERM stops a TERM object once it reaches a SCREEN COBOL ACCEPT statement with STOP-MODE set to zero and is not in TMF transaction mode.
ABORT TERM aborts a suspended or running TERM object.
Message 3001 means the SCREEN COBOL object file is corrupted or the compiler generated invalid code, and the terminal is suspended.
A wrong transfer count may indicate a terminal hardware problem, so run terminal diagnostics for the device.
START DISK makes a stopped disk accessible and can revive the half of a mirrored volume that is STOPPED, substate DOWN.
The STATUS AUDITTRAIL command displays the current audit trail activity.
The CPU parameter must be an integer from 0 through 15.
The TACL STATUS command is an alias for the #XSTATUS built-in function.
STOP TMF shuts down TMF and terminates transaction processing.
ABORT DISK deletes the disk's configuration from the SCF database.
ABORT is a nonsensitive command that any user may issue.
STOP TERM can only be issued for configured TERM objects, not temporary ones.
STOP TERM stops all disks in the PATHMON environment.
Message 3001 indicates a disk path failure, so run diagnostics on the disk.
The recovery for wrong transfer count is to restart the TMF subsystem.
The FORCED option can be used with STOP TERM to skip interactive prompts.
STATUS AUDITTRAIL permanently deletes audit trail files that are older than the DETAIL setting.
The CPU parameter may be any integer from 0 through 255.
The TACL STATUS command always requires SUPER.SUPER privileges.
STOP TMF automatically restarts TMF after the shutdown completes.
START DISK permanently deletes the data on a mirrored volume before reviving it.
